title: Enzymes and metabolism

sections.title: Catalysis and specificity
sections.body: Enzymes accelerate reactions by lowering activation energy. They do not supply the overall energy released by a reaction or change its equilibrium position. Substrates interact with an active site whose shape and chemical properties support binding and catalysis. Binding can change the shapes of both enzyme and substrate, described by induced fit. Metabolism contains many linked reactions: anabolic reactions build larger molecules, while catabolic reactions break substances down.
sections.pitfall: An enzyme makes a reaction faster; it does not make an energetically unfavourable reaction favourable simply by being present.

sections.title: Interpreting enzyme experiments
sections.body: At low substrate concentration, increasing substrate usually increases the frequency of productive interactions with active sites. At high substrate concentration, a fixed quantity of enzyme can become saturated, so rate approaches a maximum. Temperature initially increases molecular motion, but excessive heating can disrupt protein structure. Changes in pH can also affect activity. An experiment should control enzyme quantity, pH and temperature while varying the chosen independent variable and measuring an initial rate.
sections.pitfall: A plateau in a substrate-concentration experiment is not necessarily caused by denaturation.

questions.prompt: What does an enzyme lower?
questions.answer: The activation energy of a reaction
distractors: The number of atoms conserved in the reaction
The equilibrium constant in every reaction
The total amount of matter in the system
questions.explanation: Catalysts provide a lower-activation-energy route while leaving the overall reaction equilibrium unchanged.

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing substrate concentration eventually has little effect on rate when enzyme concentration is fixed.
questions.answer: At high substrate concentration, most active sites are occupied much of the time.~The amount and turnover rate of the enzyme then limit the overall reaction rate.
questions.explanation: Use saturation of a fixed enzyme supply, not an unsupported claim that substrate destroys the enzyme.

questions.prompt: An enzyme reaction produces 18 µmol of product in the first 30 seconds. Calculate the mean rate over this interval in µmol min⁻¹. State one reason to prefer an initial interval over a much later interval.
questions.answer: 30 seconds = 0.5 minutes, so rate = 18/0.5 = 36 µmol min⁻¹.~Later measurements may be affected by substrate depletion or product accumulation.
questions.explanation: Convert time before calculating rate. Initial rates reduce, but do not remove, experimental complications.

remaining: Add full reaction-energy and rate diagrams, experimental practice and HL inhibition and pathway-regulation mechanisms.

title: Cell respiration

sections.title: ATP and energy transfer
sections.body: Cell respiration transfers energy from carbon compounds into forms cells can use, including ATP. ATP is adenosine triphosphate, a nucleotide that can couple energy-releasing reactions to processes such as active transport, synthesis and movement. ATP is continually used and regenerated; it is not a long-term energy store equivalent to fat. Both producers and consumers respire, including plant cells during light and dark conditions.
sections.pitfall: Plants do not stop respiring when photosynthesis begins.

sections.title: Aerobic and anaerobic routes
sections.body: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and can release much more usable energy per glucose molecule than fermentation. A simplified overall equation is glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, with energy transferred to ATP and heat. Without enough oxygen, human muscle cells can form lactate, while yeast can produce ethanol and carbon dioxide. These routes regenerate molecules needed to keep glycolysis operating, but yield relatively little ATP per glucose compared with aerobic respiration.
sections.pitfall: Anaerobic metabolism is not the same as no ATP production.

questions.prompt: Which organisms carry out cell respiration?
questions.answer: Both autotrophs and heterotrophs
distractors: Only animals
Only non-photosynthetic organisms
Only organisms without mitochondria
questions.explanation: Autotrophs also require usable energy for cellular work and oxidize carbon compounds.

questions.prompt: Compare the products of anaerobic glucose metabolism in human muscle cells and yeast.
questions.answer: Human muscle cells can produce lactate.~Yeast can produce ethanol and carbon dioxide.~Both routes support a relatively small ATP yield from glycolysis compared with aerobic respiration.
questions.explanation: Do not assign ethanol production to human muscle cells.

questions.prompt: A respirometer records oxygen uptake by germinating seeds. An equal apparatus containing boiled seeds shows no uptake. Suggest the role of the boiled-seed comparison and one variable that must still be controlled.
questions.answer: It helps distinguish respiration by living tissue from non-biological changes in the apparatus.~Temperature, seed quantity or apparatus volume should be controlled.
questions.explanation: A control improves interpretation but does not eliminate all possible physical confounders.

remaining: Add detailed respirometry and substrate comparisons. HL glycolysis, link reaction, Krebs cycle, electron transport and chemiosmosis require dedicated lessons.

title: Photosynthesis

sections.title: Light energy and carbon fixation
sections.body: Photosynthesis uses light energy to support the production of organic compounds from carbon dioxide. In oxygenic photosynthesis, water supplies hydrogen and the oxygen released comes from water. A simplified word equation is carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light and photosynthetic pigments required. Light is the energy input, not a material incorporated into biomass. Plants also continue to respire, so measured gas exchange can be the net result of two processes.
sections.pitfall: The oxygen released in oxygenic photosynthesis does not come directly from the carbon dioxide molecules fixed into sugars.

sections.title: Pigments and limiting factors
sections.body: Pigments absorb some wavelengths more strongly than others. An absorption spectrum describes light absorption; an action spectrum describes a biological response, such as photosynthetic rate, at different wavelengths. Light intensity, carbon-dioxide availability and temperature can limit photosynthesis. Increasing one factor has little effect when another becomes limiting. Fair tests control other factors, repeat measurements and distinguish net oxygen production from gross photosynthetic activity.
sections.pitfall: A plant's green appearance does not mean that green light is its most strongly absorbed wavelength range.

questions.prompt: Where does the oxygen gas released during oxygenic photosynthesis originate?
questions.answer: Water
distractors: Glucose entering the leaf
Nitrogen in the air
The mineral ions absorbed by roots
questions.explanation: Water is split during the light-dependent processes; its oxygen atoms can be released as oxygen gas.

questions.prompt: Distinguish an absorption spectrum from an action spectrum.
questions.answer: An absorption spectrum shows how strongly a pigment or sample absorbs different wavelengths.~An action spectrum shows the effectiveness of different wavelengths in producing a biological response.
questions.explanation: Identify what is measured on the vertical axis in each case.

questions.prompt: At low light intensity, increasing light raises oxygen production. At high intensity, extra light has no effect, but adding carbon dioxide raises production. Suggest an explanation.
questions.answer: Light was limiting at low intensity.~At the higher intensity, carbon-dioxide availability became limiting.~Adding carbon dioxide removed part of that limitation.
questions.explanation: The response to changing each factor supports the inference about which factor limits rate.

remaining: Add chromatography, complete experimental analysis and HL light-dependent reactions, chemiosmosis and the Calvin cycle.

title: Chemical signalling

sections.title: Signals and target cells
sections.body: A signalling molecule affects a cell only if the cell can detect it through a suitable receptor and produce a response. Receptors have binding sites with properties that recognize particular ligands. Water-soluble signals often bind to receptors at the cell surface, while some lipid-soluble signals can cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors. Endocrine signals travel through circulation; local signalling acts over shorter distances.
sections.pitfall: A hormone reaching every tissue in the blood does not mean every cell responds to it.

sections.title: From receptor to response
sections.body: Receptor activation can trigger a sequence of intracellular events, including changes in enzyme activity, ion movement or gene expression. A cascade can amplify a small external signal because one activated component can affect several downstream components. Signalling also needs termination: ligand removal, receptor inactivation and breakdown of intermediates prevent a response from persisting indefinitely. Negative feedback reduces the initial disturbance, whereas positive feedback reinforces a change until a separate endpoint intervenes.
sections.pitfall: Signal amplification does not mean that the original hormone must enter every downstream reaction.

questions.prompt: Why might two cells exposed to the same hormone respond differently?
questions.answer: They may differ in receptors or downstream signalling machinery
distractors: Hormones always change into different elements in each cell
Only cells nearest the heart receive hormones
All receptors have identical binding properties
questions.explanation: Detection and response depend on the cell's molecular machinery, not just exposure.

questions.prompt: Explain how a signalling cascade can amplify a response.
questions.answer: One activated component can activate several molecules at the next step.~Repeated multiplication across a sequence can produce a large downstream response from a small initial signal.
questions.explanation: Amplification describes the number of affected downstream components, not creation of matter or energy.

questions.prompt: A hormone binds normally to cells with a receptor mutation, but no downstream response occurs. Suggest where the defect may act.
questions.answer: The mutation may preserve ligand binding but prevent receptor activation or coupling to downstream components.~A test of early intracellular signals could distinguish this from a later response defect.
questions.explanation: Binding and signal transduction are related but separable functions.

remaining: Add the full set of receptor classes, named pathways, steroid-hormone examples and feedback applications. All resources in this topic are HL-only.

title: Neural signalling

sections.title: Neurons and electrical signalling
sections.body: Neurons have a cell body and projecting fibres, including an axon and dendrites. A resting membrane potential reflects unequal ion distributions and selective membrane permeability. ATP-dependent pumping maintains sodium and potassium gradients; the resting interior is negative relative to the outside. A nerve impulse is a propagated action potential involving ion movement across the membrane. Conduction speed varies with properties such as axon diameter and myelination.
sections.pitfall: An impulse does not consist of one packet of neurotransmitter travelling down the entire axon.

sections.title: Chemical synapses
sections.body: At a chemical synapse, arrival of an impulse at the presynaptic terminal triggers calcium entry. Calcium promotes release of neurotransmitter from vesicles. The transmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. At an excitatory cholinergic synapse, acetylcholine can produce a postsynaptic depolarization. A typical chemical synapse transmits in one direction because release and receptor machinery occupy different sides.
sections.pitfall: The electrical impulse does not jump unchanged across a chemical synaptic cleft.

questions.prompt: What directly links presynaptic depolarization to neurotransmitter release at a typical chemical synapse?
questions.answer: Calcium entry into the presynaptic terminal
distractors: DNA replication in the synaptic cleft
Movement of the postsynaptic nucleus into the axon
Conversion of acetylcholine into an electrical wire
questions.explanation: Calcium acts as an intracellular signal promoting vesicle release.

questions.prompt: Outline how a signal crosses a chemical synapse.
questions.answer: An impulse reaches the presynaptic terminal and triggers calcium entry.~Neurotransmitter is released and diffuses across the cleft.~It binds to postsynaptic receptors and changes the activity of the postsynaptic membrane.
questions.explanation: Keep the events in order and distinguish electrical transmission along the neuron from chemical transmission between cells.

questions.prompt: An impulse travels 0.60 m in 0.010 s. Calculate conduction speed. State why comparing this value between two axons does not by itself identify the cause of a difference.
questions.answer: Speed = distance/time = 0.60/0.010 = 60 m s⁻¹.~Diameter, myelination, temperature or other conditions may differ, so relevant variables must be controlled.
questions.explanation: A numerical difference is an observation; identifying its cause requires controlled comparison.

remaining: Core mechanisms are introduced. Add required correlation analysis and HL action-potential phases, local currents, saltatory conduction, inhibitory signalling and summation.

title: Integration of body systems

sections.title: Coordinating multiple systems
sections.body: Cells form tissues, organs and organ systems whose activities must be coordinated. Nervous signals can target particular effectors rapidly; hormones can coordinate responses in cells with suitable receptors. Circulation transports gases, nutrients, hormones and waste between organs. During exercise, muscles, ventilation and circulation interact: greater metabolic activity increases demand for oxygen and delivery of respiratory substrates while carbon dioxide must be removed.
sections.pitfall: An organ's function cannot always be understood in isolation from the systems supplying and regulating it.

sections.title: Receptors, integration and effectors
sections.body: A coordinated response can be described as detection by a receptor, information processing by an integrating system and action by an effector. The brain combines inputs and participates in learning and memory. Reflex pathways can generate rapid responses without waiting for a conscious decision. An effector may be a muscle or gland. The result can then alter the input, completing a feedback loop when the response influences the monitored variable.
sections.pitfall: A rapid reflex is not evidence that the nervous system is absent from the response.

questions.prompt: Which is an effector in a withdrawal response?
questions.answer: A skeletal muscle that contracts
distractors: A receptor detecting the damaging stimulus
The external hot surface
A sensory input before processing
questions.explanation: An effector carries out the response; a receptor detects the stimulus.

questions.prompt: Explain why increased muscle activity requires coordination with the circulatory system.
questions.answer: Active muscle requires delivery of oxygen and respiratory substrates.~It also produces carbon dioxide and other substances that must be transported away.~Circulatory adjustments help match transport to the altered demand.
questions.explanation: Link muscular metabolism to transport rather than simply listing two systems.

questions.prompt: Cardiac output is heart rate × stroke volume. Calculate output when heart rate is 120 beats min⁻¹ and stroke volume is 90 mL beat⁻¹, then express it in L min⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The beat units cancel. The supplied equation makes this a transport application rather than a recall test of a new formula.

remaining: Add full named nervous and endocrine control pathways, required brain and spinal-cord details and HL plant integration.

title: Defence against disease

sections.title: Barriers and innate defence
sections.body: Pathogens can cause infectious disease. Skin and mucous membranes limit entry; secretions and physical removal mechanisms can reduce the chance of infection. If barriers are breached, innate responses include inflammation and phagocytosis. Phagocytes engulf material and digest it in intracellular compartments. Innate defence responds to broad features and does not require a previous encounter with that specific pathogen.
sections.pitfall: Not all microorganisms are pathogens, and inflammation does not identify one particular cause by itself.

sections.title: Specific responses and memory
sections.body: Adaptive responses depend on recognition of particular antigens. Activated lymphocyte populations expand; some descendants produce antibodies and others become memory cells. Antibodies bind specific targets and can assist neutralization or removal. A later encounter can trigger a faster and stronger response because memory cells are already available. Vaccination exposes the immune system to suitable antigenic information without requiring the person to experience the full target disease.
sections.pitfall: Antibodies are proteins; they are not cells that engulf pathogens.

questions.prompt: Which process involves a cell engulfing and digesting material?
questions.answer: Phagocytosis
distractors: Antibody binding by itself
Ventilation
Transcription
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis is a cellular uptake-and-digestion process, unlike the binding action of an antibody molecule.

questions.prompt: Explain why a secondary immune response can be faster than the primary response.
questions.answer: The first response can produce antigen-specific memory cells.~On re-exposure, these cells can respond and expand more rapidly, producing an effective response sooner.
questions.explanation: Connect memory-cell persistence to the timing of the later response.

questions.prompt: After vaccination, antibody concentration rises and later falls. A student concludes that all protection disappears as soon as the concentration begins to fall. Evaluate the conclusion.
questions.answer: Falling circulating antibody concentration does not by itself show that all protection has vanished.~Memory cells and other immune components may persist.~Protection against a particular outcome requires relevant evidence, not only the direction of one measurement.
questions.explanation: Avoid treating one biomarker as a complete measure of immune protection.

remaining: Add the full range of pathogens, blood clotting, antibiotic resistance, disease examples and HL immune mechanisms.

title: Populations and communities

sections.title: Population change and limits
sections.body: A population is a group of organisms of one species in an area; a community contains interacting populations of different species. Births and immigration add individuals, while deaths and emigration remove them. Population growth can slow when resources or space become limiting. Carrying capacity describes a population size an environment can sustain under particular conditions; it can change when conditions change rather than remaining permanently fixed.
sections.pitfall: A community contains multiple populations, not merely a large population of one species.

sections.title: Sampling and interactions
sections.body: Quadrats sample sessile organisms or slow-moving organisms in a defined area. Random placement reduces deliberate site-selection bias; systematic sampling along a transect can investigate a gradient. Replication helps estimate variation. Organisms also interact through competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism and mutualism. An observed correlation between two populations does not by itself establish the interaction or direction of causation.
sections.pitfall: More quadrats do not remove bias if all are placed only in convenient or unusually dense patches.

questions.prompt: Which change directly increases population size, with other processes unchanged?
questions.answer: Immigration
distractors: Emigration
Deaths
A decrease in births
questions.explanation: Immigration adds individuals to the defined population.

questions.prompt: Explain why random quadrat placement and replication address different problems.
questions.answer: Random placement reduces systematic site-selection bias.~Replication samples variation and improves the basis for estimating abundance and uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Repeated biased sampling can still give a misleading estimate.

questions.prompt: Five randomly placed quadrats of 0.25 m² contain 3, 5, 4, 6 and 2 plants. Estimate the number of plants in a comparable 100 m² area, and state one assumption.
questions.answer: Mean = 20/5 = 4 plants per quadrat, or 16 plants m⁻².~Estimated total = 16 × 100 = 1,600 plants.~The sampled quadrats must adequately represent the larger area.
questions.explanation: This is an estimate with sampling uncertainty, not an exact census.

remaining: There is no additional HL content, but required population models, interaction examples, statistical association and allelopathy or antibiotic-secretion applications still need expansion.

title: Transfers of energy and matter

sections.title: Open systems and energy inputs
sections.body: An open ecosystem exchanges both matter and energy with its surroundings. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter; it is not necessarily isolated from light or heat. Sunlight supports most ecosystems through photosynthesis. Some deep environments instead rely on chemical energy, and a dark cave may receive organic material made by photosynthesis outside it. Define the system boundary before deciding whether an input is direct or imported.
sections.pitfall: A closed bottle can still receive light and lose heat; closed does not mean isolated.

sections.title: Food chains, webs and decomposers
sections.body: Food-chain arrows point from a resource toward the consumer receiving its biomass and chemical energy. For example: grass → grasshopper → frog. A food web joins several chains because organisms can have multiple foods and predators. Dead leaves, carcasses and faeces contain organic compounds that supply decomposers and detritus feeders. These routes connect material from many trophic levels to decomposition rather than forming only one final link after the top predator.
sections.pitfall: A food-web arrow does not normally point from the hunter toward what it catches.

sections.title: Carbon sources and energy sources
sections.body: Autotrophs build organic compounds from inorganic carbon using an external energy supply. Photoautotrophs use light; chemoautotrophs use energy from chemical oxidation, such as the oxidation of iron compounds by some bacteria. Heterotrophs obtain organic carbon from other organisms and use it to build their own molecules. Both groups respire, transferring energy from carbon compounds into ATP and heat. Being a producer does not remove the need for respiration.
sections.pitfall: Autotroph does not mean an organism creates energy or matter from nothing.

sections.title: Trophic levels and energy pyramids
sections.body: Producers occupy the first trophic level. Primary consumers feed on producers, secondary consumers feed on primary consumers, and tertiary consumers feed on secondary consumers. An omnivore can occupy different levels in different chains. An energy pyramid compares energy transferred per unit area per unit time, such as kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. Use one common scale and period across levels. Unlike a snapshot of standing biomass, an energy-flow pyramid records a rate over time.
sections.pitfall: An organism is not necessarily assigned one permanent trophic level regardless of what it eats.

sections.title: Why transfer is incomplete
sections.body: Not all biomass is eaten, and not everything eaten is digested and assimilated. Some energy therefore passes into detritus rather than into the next consumer's new biomass. Organisms also respire and dissipate energy as heat during ATP production and use. Energy available to build biomass at successive feeding levels consequently declines, limiting the length of food chains. Transfer efficiency varies: 10% is a convenient example, not a universal fixed biological law.
sections.pitfall: Energy is conserved, but heat dispersed into the surroundings is not recycled into food by the ecosystem's organisms.

sections.title: Primary and secondary production
sections.body: Primary production is the accumulation of organic carbon compounds in autotroph biomass; secondary production is accumulation in heterotroph biomass. Report production as mass or energy per unit area per unit time, not simply as the mass present on one date. Growth and reproduction add biomass, while respiration transfers some carbon back to the environment. A consumer's intake is therefore not equivalent to its new biomass production. When a problem distinguishes gross from net production, subtract the specified respiratory cost to obtain net production.
sections.pitfall: Standing biomass is a stock; production is a rate. Their units and interpretations differ.

sections.title: Tracing carbon through an ecosystem
sections.body: A carbon-cycle diagram should label both stores and processes. Atmospheric carbon dioxide → photosynthesis → plant organic compounds → feeding → animal organic compounds. Respiration by plants, animals and decomposers returns carbon dioxide. Death and egestion move organic material toward detrital stores. These arrows represent movements of carbon atoms, unlike arrows describing energy dissipation. Mineral nutrients and other required elements also cycle, with decomposers helping return them to available forms.
sections.pitfall: Decomposers recycle matter, not the same usable energy indefinitely.

sections.title: Carbon sinks, sources and gas exchange
sections.body: A system is a carbon sink over a stated interval when its net carbon uptake exceeds its release, and a source when release exceeds uptake. In a simplified ecosystem budget, photosynthetic carbon uptake exceeding total respiration gives net uptake; other exports, imports and disturbances can alter a real budget. Oxygenic photosynthesis supplies oxygen used by aerobic respiration, while respiration supplies carbon dioxide available for photosynthesis. These large opposing flows can occur at the same time.
sections.pitfall: A forest is not automatically a carbon sink in every year merely because its trees photosynthesize.

sections.title: Combustion and long-term carbon stores
sections.body: Combustion of biomass, peat and fossil fuels converts stored carbon into products including carbon dioxide. These stores accumulated over very different timescales. Burning them can release stored carbon much more rapidly than it is replaced. Fire can begin naturally, but human activities have greatly increased fossil-carbon release. Describing a carbon budget requires both the rate of release and the rates of uptake or storage, not only the existence of one process.
sections.pitfall: A carbon store and a carbon sink are not identical ideas: a large store can be losing carbon.

sections.title: Interpreting seasonal and long-term change
sections.body: The Keeling Curve records atmospheric carbon-dioxide concentration over time. Its seasonal oscillation reflects changing net biological uptake and release, strongly influenced by the Northern Hemisphere's land vegetation. During active growth, uptake can lower atmospheric concentration; seasonal slowing of growth changes the balance. The multi-decade increase is a separate feature associated with net additions of carbon dioxide, especially from human activities. Describe the long-term trend and the oscillation separately before explaining them.
sections.pitfall: A seasonal fall does not disprove a rising long-term trend.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes a closed system rather than an isolated system?
questions.answer: Energy can cross its boundary, but matter does not
distractors: Neither matter nor energy can cross its boundary
Matter can cross but energy never can
It must remain at a constant temperature
questions.explanation: Closed refers to matter exchange. Energy exchange remains possible.

questions.prompt: A grasshopper eats grass. Which arrow follows the usual food-chain convention?
questions.answer: Grass → grasshopper
distractors: Grasshopper → grass
Grass ↔ grasshopper to indicate the direction of feeding energy
No arrow because plants do not contain chemical energy
questions.explanation: The arrow follows transfer of biomass and energy from the food to its consumer.

questions.prompt: Compare photoautotrophs and chemoautotrophs.
questions.answer: Both can synthesize organic compounds from inorganic carbon.~Photoautotrophs use light as an energy source.~Chemoautotrophs use energy from chemical oxidation reactions.
questions.explanation: Separate their shared carbon strategy from their different energy sources.

questions.prompt: A bird eats seeds and also insects that feed on seeds. Explain why the bird can occupy more than one trophic level.
questions.answer: When eating seeds from producers, it acts as a primary consumer.~When eating seed-eating insects, it acts as a secondary consumer.
questions.explanation: Assign the level using the particular feeding route.

questions.prompt: Annual energy transfer is 24,000 kJ m⁻² to primary consumers and 3,600 kJ m⁻² to secondary consumers. Calculate transfer efficiency between these levels.
questions.answer: Efficiency = 3600/24000 × 100 = 15%.~Both measurements use the same area and time interval, so they are comparable.
questions.explanation: Use output divided by input, not the inverse. The result illustrates why assuming a universal 10% transfer would be wrong.

questions.prompt: Explain two routes by which energy in producer biomass fails to become new primary-consumer biomass.
questions.answer: Some producer material is not eaten, or eaten material is not assimilated and enters detrital pathways.~Some assimilated energy is used in respiration and dissipated as heat rather than retained in new biomass.
questions.explanation: Distinguish transfer to detritus from dissipation as heat.

questions.prompt: A producer community fixes 1,100 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹ and returns 420 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹ through its own respiration. Using net production = gross fixation − producer respiration, calculate net production.
questions.answer: Net production = 1100 − 420 = 680 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The formula and the definition of the respiration term are supplied. Do not subtract unrelated consumer respiration in this calculation.

questions.prompt: A consumer ingests 800 kJ, loses 240 kJ in unassimilated material and dissipates 420 kJ through respiratory processes over the same interval. Assuming no other losses or storage changes, determine energy retained as new biomass.
questions.answer: Retained energy = 800 − 240 − 420 = 140 kJ.
questions.explanation: Ingestion is not production; subtract the specified losses before identifying the retained component.

questions.prompt: Outline a carbon pathway from atmospheric carbon dioxide into a herbivore and back to the atmosphere.
questions.answer: Photosynthesis incorporates atmospheric carbon into plant organic compounds.~The herbivore obtains this carbon by feeding and assimilation.~Respiration returns some carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: Name stores and processes in the correct sequence.

questions.prompt: Explain why an ecosystem can recycle chemical elements but needs a continuing energy input.
questions.answer: Atoms can move between organisms and environmental stores and be reused in new compounds.~Energy transfers disperse some energy as heat, which is not returned to the same usable biological pathways.~An external input replaces the usable energy dissipated.
questions.explanation: Conservation of energy does not imply that all forms remain equally available for cellular work.

questions.prompt: Over one year, an ecosystem takes up 900 tonnes of carbon through photosynthesis and releases 970 tonnes through total respiration. Ignore other carbon fluxes. Determine whether it is a net sink or source and calculate the net flux.
questions.answer: Release exceeds uptake by 970 − 900 = 70 tonnes of carbon per year.~It is a net source under the stated simplified budget.
questions.explanation: The classification depends on the balance over the specified interval, not simply on the presence of photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Explain why burning a long-established peat deposit can increase atmospheric carbon dioxide rapidly.
questions.answer: The peat contains organic carbon accumulated over a long interval.~Combustion oxidizes stored carbon and releases carbon dioxide much faster than the store may be replaced.
questions.explanation: Link the pre-existing store, the combustion process and the imbalance in timescales.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical annual CO₂ series reaches 410 ppm in spring and 404 ppm in autumn in year 1, then 413 ppm in spring and 407 ppm in autumn in year 2. Describe the seasonal pattern and the year-to-year change separately.
questions.answer: Within each year, the spring value exceeds the autumn value by 6 ppm.~At the same season, year 2 is 3 ppm higher than year 1.~A seasonal decline therefore coexists with a rising year-to-year baseline.
questions.explanation: These are explicitly hypothetical data, not current measurements from the Keeling Curve.

questions.prompt: Explain one gas-exchange interdependence between photosynthesis and aerobic respiration.
questions.answer: Oxygenic photosynthesis releases oxygen that aerobic respiration can consume.~Respiration releases carbon dioxide that photosynthesis can incorporate into organic compounds.
questions.explanation: Both processes can operate within the same organism as well as between different trophic groups.

remaining: All 22 numbered understandings have relevant original teaching. Full coverage is not certified: students still need researched local food webs, scaled energy-pyramid construction, actual carbon-cycle drawing, source-data interpretation and teacher-reviewed assessment depth. There is no additional HL content in C4.2.
